newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: New Philippine Senate head vows to pass tax bill.
newsitem.headline: New Philippine Senate head vows to pass tax bill.

text.p: New Philippine Senate president Ernesto Maceda pledged on Wednesday that a tax reform bill on cigarettes and beer would be passed within the year.

Maceda, voted into the Senate presidency last week by opposition parties, told reporters after a meeting with government officials and top legislators that the Senate will approve its version of the bill within the week.

The Senate version of the bill, a crucial but contentious element in a major tax reform package, will then be reconciled in a bicameral committee with one passed earlier by the House of Representatives.
The final version would be passed within the year, Maceda said.
"We're ready to push it to its conclusion," Maceda said. The Congress is scheduled to start a two-week recess on Friday.
Finance Secretary Roberto de Ocampo told a news conference that he was heartened that the proposed Senate bill closely followed what the administration has envisioned.

The government wants to do away with a much abused ad valorem system for calculating excise taxes. Some manufacturers have been accused of misrepresenting the value of their products, which forms the bases for the advalorem tax.
The specific tax system is based on volume and is much simpler to administer.
The House of Representatives bill would allow the government to either tax the products based on value or volume, whichever is higher.
The House version is estimated to bring in only 4.06 billion pesos in the first three years of implementation against 7.0 billion for the Senate version.
The finance ministry has dismissed the House version as being too complicated and too open to tax evasion.
The excise tax is one of the major components of the government's Comprehensive Tax Reform Package which was first put forward more than two years ago.
The International Monetary Fund has urged the package's speedy passage as proceeds from a government privatisation programme are expected to dwindle in the next couple of years.
